result: STIM1 and Orai1 puncta accumulate in the center of the immune synapse (ADZ) after cells spread, with some puncta moving centripetally from the periphery at ~47 nm/s.
evaluation: Claims C41-C47 are supported by quantitative imaging data showing STIM1/Orai1 puncta centralization (68/82 cells), centripetal movement (27/68 cells), and measured velocities (47±3 nm/s). The interpretation that ER-PM junctions concentrate in the ADZ is consistent with the imaging observations.

result: STIM1 puncta in the lamella move centripetally with F-actin at the same velocity, suggesting actin flow transports STIM1/Orai1 puncta and ER-PM junctions toward the ADZ.
evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by kymograph analysis (Figure 1E) showing STIM1 and actin moving together at similar velocities. The interpretation that actin flow drives STIM1/Orai1 movement is a reasonable inference from the correlated motion.

result: ER tubules extend from the ADZ toward the periphery on microtubules (with EB1 at tips), but rarely enter the lamellipod because microtubules cannot penetrate this actin-dense compartment.
evaluation: Claims C54-C64 are supported by imaging data showing ER dynamics (20/20 cells with ADZ enrichment, 16/20 with extending tubules), EB1 localization at tubule tips, and EB1 reorientation at the lamellipod/lamella border. The interpretation about microtubule exclusion is consistent with observations and prior literature.

result: ER tubules undergoing retrograde movement are sandwiched between actin arcs and move at the same velocity, indicating that retrograde actin flow sweeps ER-PM junctions into the ADZ.
evaluation: Claims C65-C68 are supported by imaging data (17/20 cells) and kymograph analysis showing coordinated ER and actin movement. The similar velocities of STIM1/Orai1 puncta (47±3 nm/s) and lamellar actin (36±6 nm/s) support the conclusion that actin flow drives ER corralling.

result: Ca2+ removal causes rapid loss of lamellipod/lamella organization, reduced ruffling, uniform F-actin distribution, and severely reduced centripetal actin movement in Jurkat cells; effects are reversible and reproduced by 2-APB.
evaluation: Claims C69-C77 are supported by quantitative imaging data (38/45 cells showing changes, 11/14 with 2-APB). STICS analysis demonstrates reduced and disorganized actin flow. The reversibility and 2-APB control support the conclusion that Ca2+ influx through CRAC channels regulates actin organization.

result: Primary human T lymphoblasts respond similarly to Jurkat cells: Ca2+ removal slows actin flow by 44%, narrows the lamellipod by 61%, and alters actin distribution; effects are reversible.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by quantitative measurements from primary T cells (20/21 cells, Table 1). The similar responses in both cell types validate the use of Jurkat cells as a model system and demonstrate physiological relevance of the findings.

result: Ca2+ influx promotes retrograde actin flow that corrals peripheral ER tubules back to the synapse center, as evidenced by ER tubule reappearance in the TIRF field upon Ca2+ readdition.
evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are supported by imaging data (6/6 cells) showing ER tubule dynamics in response to Ca2+ manipulations. The interpretation that Ca2+ promotes ER corralling through actin flow is consistent with the observed coordinated movement of ER and actin.

result: Blocking Ca2+ influx increases F-actin density by 20-30%, with F-actin levels highly correlated with [Ca2+]i (R²=0.83) but not [Ca2+]o (R²=0.22), demonstrating that intracellular Ca2+ reversibly regulates F-actin density.
evaluation: Claims C85-C91 are supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements from both TIRF and confocal microscopy, simultaneous Ca2+ and actin imaging (n=26 cells), and correlation analysis. The high R² value and reversibility demonstrate a robust Ca2+-dependent regulation of F-actin density.

result: Ca2+ removal decreases actin velocity by 41% in the lamellipod and 64% in the lamella, and extends actin filament half-life by 17-23%, indicating that Ca2+ influx accelerates actin depolymerization.
evaluation: Claims C92-C95 are supported by photoactivation experiments with quantitative measurements (Table 2, n=10-19 cells). The increased half-life upon Ca2+ removal directly demonstrates that Ca2+ accelerates depolymerization. Controls for perfusion artifacts strengthen the conclusion.

result: Ca2+ regulates F-actin density and depolymerization independently of myosin, as blebbistatin treatment does not prevent the 30% increase in F-actin density upon Ca2+ removal.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97 are supported by experiments showing similar Ca2+ effects on F-actin density in the presence of blebbistatin (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). This control experiment effectively rules out myosin as the primary mediator of Ca2+ effects on actin depolymerization.

result: In the absence of Ca2+, photoactivated actin incorporates throughout the synapse within 3s, but in the presence of Ca2+, incorporation is restricted to a narrow peripheral band within 2s, demonstrating that Ca2+ promotes polymerization at the lamellipod edge while suppressing it elsewhere.
evaluation: Claims C98-C103 are supported by photoactivation experiments (n=12-13 cells) showing dramatically different spatial patterns of actin incorporation depending on Ca2+ presence. The selective peripheral incorporation in Ca2+ provides direct evidence for Ca2+-dependent spatial restriction of polymerization.

result: Ca2+ enriches WAVE2 and Abi1 at the synapse periphery; Ca2+ removal causes reversible diffuse distribution of Abi1, suggesting Ca2+ restricts actin polymerization to the periphery by controlling nucleation location.
evaluation: Claims C104-C107 are supported by immunocytochemistry (n=63 cells each condition) and live-cell imaging of EGFP-Abi1 (n=8 cells). The correlation between WAVE2/Abi1 localization and actin polymerization patterns supports the interpretation about Ca2+-dependent control of nucleation sites.

result: Ca2+ influx is required to drive actin organization and dynamics at the synapse by promoting depolymerization, localizing polymerization and WAVE2 to the periphery, and suppressing polymerization elsewhere, which in turn drives ER remodeling and CRAC channel localization.
evaluation: This integrative result synthesizes multiple supported findings (C5-C9, C13, C108-C109, C112) demonstrating Ca2+ acts at multiple levels to organize actin. The conclusion is well-supported by the collective experimental evidence from photoactivation, imaging, and localization studies.

result: Ca2+-dependent retrograde actin flow corrals ER tubules and STIM1/Orai1 complexes to the synapse center, creating a self-organizing process for CRAC channel localization at the ADZ.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12, C110, C126, C128 are supported by imaging data showing coordinated movement of ER, STIM1/Orai1, and actin at similar velocities, and the Ca2+-dependent nature of this process. The self-organization concept is a reasonable interpretation of the positive feedback between Ca2+ influx and actin-mediated CRAC channel concentration.

result: Ca2+ influx may modulate TCR signaling through feedback loops: promoting actin turnover creates positive feedback to maintain CRAC channel activation, while accelerating microcluster transport to the cSMAC limits their signaling lifetime.
evaluation: Claims C14, C122-C125 are speculative interpretations about functional consequences. While the observations about Ca2+ effects on actin and CRAC channel localization are well-supported, the proposed feedback loops and effects on TCR signaling are not directly tested. These remain plausible hypotheses requiring further validation.

result: Potential mechanisms for Ca2+ effects include PI3K/PIP3-mediated WAVE2 recruitment, Rac activation, and Ca2+-sensitive capping proteins (gelsolin, CapG) or severing proteins (cofilin, gelsolin) rather than myosin.
evaluation: Claims C114-C117 are largely speculative mechanisms based on prior literature. While myosin is ruled out by blebbistatin experiments (C117), the other proposed mechanisms are not directly tested. These represent reasonable hypotheses for future investigation but lack direct experimental support in this study.

result: Background knowledge about immune synapse structure, TCR signaling, actin organization, CRAC channel activation, and Ca2+ effects on T cell behavior.
evaluation: Claims C1-C38 represent established knowledge from prior literature, appropriately cited. These provide the necessary context for the current study and are well-supported by the cited references. No evaluation of new experimental findings is required for these background claims.

result: Methodological observations about cell spreading, STIM1/Orai1 puncta appearance, and actin organization into lamellipod/lamella with retrograde flow velocities of ~100 nm/s declining to 0 nm/s at the ADZ border.
evaluation: Claims C39-C40, C48-C50 describe basic experimental observations consistent with prior literature and serve to establish the experimental system. These are well-documented observations that validate the model system used in the study.

result: Discussion of prior work on Ca2+ and actin, ER dynamics, CRAC channel self-organization mechanisms, and potential functional significance for cytokine secretion.
evaluation: Claims C111, C118-C121, C127, C129 appropriately summarize and contextualize prior work (C111, C121, C127) and offer reasonable interpretations (C118-C120) or speculation (C129) about functional significance. These discussion points are appropriately qualified and supported by citations.
